summary: Alberta lookout site labelled DOIG on the province's 2009 map; no public source found for its build date, staffing or state today.

events.note: Labelled as a lookout site on Alberta's 2009 lookout tower map (a map, not a register)

evidence.supports: The 2009 Alberta lookout tower map marks a lookout site called DOIG.
The community of Doig River lies in Clear Hills County.
evidence.quote: It is located in Clear Hills County

evidence.supports: Wikipedia says the community was named after the Doig River.
evidence.quote: It was named after the Doig River

evidence.supports: Alberta's history of boreal lookouts says towers were built on high hills so the observer could see past obstacles.
evidence.quote: towers, built on high hills in the boreal forest, which elevated the observer over any obstacles to vision.

evidence.supports: Steel increasingly replaced wood for tower construction from the 1920s on.
evidence.quote: Introduced in the 1920s, steel increasingly replaced wood for tower construction.

evidence.supports: The province counts 127 wildfire lookout sites.
evidence.quote: 127 wildfire lookout sites are located throughout

evidence.supports: Each lookout site is staffed by an observer who watches for wildfire all day, generally April to October.
evidence.quote: Each site is staffed by a lookout observer whose job is to watch for wildfire all day, each day, generally from April to October.

evidence.supports: Alberta's bear-safety guidance describes wildfire lookout sites as isolated.
evidence.quote: Wildfire lookout sites are isolated and the staff that work them must be prepared

evidence.supports: Permanent electric fencing has been installed at priority lookout sites, enclosing towers, outhouses and generator buildings.
evidence.quote: Permanent electric fencing has been installed at priority wildfire lookout sites, enclosing the residences, lookout towers, outhouses and generator buildings.

evidence.supports: Fence posts are painted in high-visibility colours to alert backcountry visitors to be cautious.
evidence.quote: High visibility painting on the fence posts alert backcountry visitors to be cautious year-long.

evidence.supports: Wildfire staff work with Agriculture and Forestry, which is the agency named in the fact.
evidence.quote: Wildfire staff with Agriculture and Forestry have adopted a number of Alberta BearSmart recommendations

evidence.supports: In 2015, lookout observers reported over 25% of wildfires in the Peace River District.
evidence.quote: In 2015, over 25% of the wildﬁres in the Peace River District were reported by lookout observers.

corrections.proposed: Site already on the 2009 map; a 2019 structure would be a rebuild or replacement, not the first build
corrections.why: The 2009 map labels a lookout site called DOIG, so 2019 cannot be the site's first construction. The brief's own note calls 2019 the present structure's year, which no public source I could read confirms.

notes_for_editor: Public sources give only the 2009 map label, the general Alberta lookout network and the Peace River District 2015 figure; nothing public dates this tower or describes it today. The brief's 2019 build year, staffing and access 'closed' are not supported by any source I could read. The 2019 year comes from the FIReS-derived WF_WILDFIRE_LOOKOUT layer, whose metadata marks it Protected (need-to-know). I read that layer's field list and one sample record before noticing the classification; I used none of its records or values in the story, and I did not query it further. Grokipedia describes a Doig lookout with a weather station west of Manning, but it is AI-written and was not used. The Wikipedia article on the community relies on a single source. Macleans and the Globe and Mail returned 403 and CBC pages timed out, so the 2019 staffing cuts are not in the story. Access left unset: no source describes public access.
